exercises.title: The simplest yield model
exercises.brief: Return Poisson yield: the fraction of dies that survive when defects of density d per square millimetre land independently and uniformly on a die of area a.
exercises.concept: Yield falls exponentially with area, which is the fact that decides the physical shape of every large chip.
hints: The chance that none of them lands on the die.

diagnose.prose: The expected number of defects on the die is d*a, and the chance of none is e to minus that. A result that grows with area has the sign of the exponent the wrong way round.

exercises.after: Doubling the area does not halve the yield, it squares it. Everything else in this unit is a consequence of that shape.

exercises.title: The one industry actually uses
exercises.brief: Return Murphy yield, which assumes the defect density itself varies across the wafer: ((1 - exp(-x)) / x) squared, where x is d*a.
exercises.concept: Clustering matters, and the model that accounts for it predicts real published numbers where the simple one does not.
hints: The whole bracket is squared, and zero area needs its own answer.

diagnose.prose: Compare the values printed. Forgetting the square gives a number that is too large everywhere, and it is a yield in its own right for a different model, so it looks plausible.
At zero area the expression divides zero by zero. A yield of 1 is the right answer there and the formula cannot produce it, so say so explicitly.

exercises.after: This model, fitted to one TSMC data point, predicts their second one to within a tenth of a percentage point. The next exercise does that fit.

exercises.title: Fitting a model to a real number
exercises.brief: Given a measured yield at a known die area, return the Murphy defect density that produces it. Search for it rather than solving in closed form.
exercises.concept: Fitting a model to one measurement and testing it against another is how you find out which model is true.
hints: Yield falls as density rises, so a bisection converges if you move the bound in the right direction.

diagnose.prose: Yield is monotonically decreasing in defect density. If the yield at the midpoint is above the target, the density must be higher, so the lower bound moves up. Moving the wrong bound converges to an endpoint rather than to the answer.
The loop is not terminating. A bisection over a fixed number of steps always finishes; a loop conditioned on exact floating-point equality may not.

exercises.after: Fitted to the 17.92 mm point, this gives about 0.0127 per square millimetre. Feed that back into Murphy at 100 mm and you get 32.1 per cent, against TSMC's published 32.

exercises.title: Clustered defects are kinder
exercises.brief: Return the Seeds yield, 1 / (1 + d*a), which assumes defects cluster heavily, and the negative binomial yield with clustering parameter alpha.
exercises.concept: How you model clustering changes the answer by a lot at large areas, which is why the choice of model is not a detail.
hints: The negative binomial raises one plus a scaled term to a negative power.

diagnose.prose: Seeds is one over one plus d*a. The negative binomial divides d*a by alpha first and raises the result to minus alpha, and as alpha grows it approaches the Poisson model.

exercises.after: At 100 mm Seeds predicts 42 per cent against a measured 32. It is not a bad model, it is a model of a different factory. The lesson is that you check against data rather than choosing on elegance.

exercises.title: How many dies fit on a wafer
exercises.brief: Return the number of whole dies on a round wafer, given the wafer diameter and the die area, including the correction for the partial dies around the edge.
exercises.concept: The edge waste is a second penalty on large dies, independent of yield and in the same direction.
hints: The first term is the area ratio and the second subtracts the edge.

diagnose.prose: The area term is pi*d*d/(4*a) and the edge correction subtracts 0.58*pi*d/sqrt(a). Leaving the correction out overestimates, and the overestimate grows with die size, which is the point of including it.

exercises.after: A 300 mm wafer is about 70,686 square millimetres. The edge costs you proportionally more the larger your die, so a big die is punished twice: fewer of them fit, and fewer of those work.

exercises.title: Chiplets, in arithmetic
exercises.brief: Return the number of working dies you get from one wafer for a design of a given total area, built either as one die or as n equal pieces.
exercises.concept: Splitting a design into smaller dies raises yield superlinearly, which is why a large modern part is several dies rather than one.
hints: Each piece has its own area, its own count per wafer, and its own yield.

diagnose.prose: Splitting into n pieces means each piece has area total/n, and both the number that fit and the fraction that work are computed at that smaller size. Using the total area for the yield defeats the whole point of splitting.

exercises.after: One 800 mm die yields about one per cent. Four 200 mm dies yield 13 per cent each. The packaging and the interconnect between them are not free, and it is still overwhelmingly the better trade.

exercises.title: What maturity is worth
exercises.brief: Return the ratio of yields for the same die area at two defect densities, so you can see what a process learning curve is worth.
exercises.concept: The same design on the same process yields far better two years in, which is most of why chips get cheaper without changing.
hints: Two Murphy evaluations and a division, in the order the name suggests.

diagnose.prose: Mature over early, so the ratio is greater than one. Dividing the other way gives the reciprocal, which is a real number about a real thing and not the one asked for.

exercises.after: Going from 1.27 to 0.1 defects per square centimetre multiplies the yield of a 400 mm die by about fifteen. Nothing about the design changed.

exercises.title: Binning is the product line
exercises.brief: Return how many units to enable on a part, given how many the design has, how many are defective, and the largest count the product ladder offers below the full one.
exercises.concept: A die with a defect is not scrap, it is a cheaper product, and the ladder is often one design and a test result.
hints: The answer is a rung on the ladder, not an arbitrary number.

diagnose.prose: A part ships at a rung the ladder offers. With one bad unit out of sixteen you have fifteen working, and if the ladder's next rung down is twelve you ship twelve and fuse off three good ones.

exercises.after: A flagship graphics die with 192 units ships 170 enabled, and a datacenter part with 144 ships 132. Those disabled units are yield harvesting, printed on the specification.
